title: Only three terminal statuses exist; there is no run-level "failed"
detail: askme.py:4162-4187 `_RunController.run()` loops `for replan in range(self.max_replans)`, calls `self.completion.try_finish(replan)` (4176) when `_execute_tasks` returns True, and falls through to `self.completion.exhausted()` (4180) otherwise. `RunOutcome.status` is documented as `"complete" | "complete_unverified" | "exhausted"` (askme.py:2927) and `COMPLETE_STATUSES = ("complete", "complete_unverified")` (askme.py:4751-4752). `task_failed` (askme.py:4312-4319) is a per-task JSONL event only and never becomes a run status. `complete_unverified` is produced at askme.py:3798-3812 when the validator is unavailable or malformed — deliberately not claiming "validation passed" from missing evidence. Public wording must therefore say runs end complete / complete_unverified / exhausted, never that a run "failed".

next_step: Fix the vocabulary in any blog/README text: three statuses, and `exhausted` is the only non-completing one.

title: An explicit model `done` is the ONLY general way a task is accepted
detail: `_decide_step` routes `done` to `_handle_done` (askme.py:4546-4547). `_handle_done` (askme.py:4560-4568) consults `self.obligations.refuse_done(ctx)` then `self.step_policy.guard_done(ctx, attempt)`; if both pass it sets `attempt.done = True` and returns END_ATTEMPT. The default policy arm is `heuristic` (askme.py:537 `DEFAULT_STEP_POLICY = _validated_step_policy(os.environ.get("AGENT_STEP_POLICY", "heuristic"))`) whose base `guard_done` returns None (askme.py:2997-2999) — so in the default arm `done` is accepted whenever no incomplete-write obligation blocks it. The consequence is the whole issue: no `done`, no completed task, regardless of what actually landed on disk.
evidence: /home/user/askme/askme.py:4546-4568 | /home/user/askme/askme.py:2997-2999 | /home/user/askme/askme.py:537 | /home/user/askme/askme.py:4276-4321
next_step: Name this explicitly in the blog post as a design choice, and decide whether receipt-backed acceptance (finding below) is the fix.

title: THE MISSING MECHANISM: no recorded evidence of a prior successful check can satisfy a verification task
detail: Answering the question plainly: there is no such path. The single receipt-backed auto-completion is `_task_satisfied_by_deterministic_repair(task, state)` (askme.py:2459-2480+), called once at askme.py:4348, and it is triple-gated — the task text must contain "include" plus one of add/insert/edit/include/fix, the requested include must be `#include <stdio.h>` or `#include <string.h>`, and a prior step must carry the `deterministic_repair` flag. It is the #41 C-header ablation, nothing more. It is further refused when the policy arm has an open verification obligation (`allows_deterministic_completion`, askme.py:3465-3468, base at 3001-3006). `_deterministic_check` (askme.py:2185+) does inspect recorded shell/write history, but it is only reachable from run-level `_validate_completion` (askme.py:2244-2252) AFTER every task already completed — it can never rescue a task that failed. And `CompletionPolicy.exhausted()` (askme.py:3840-3856) documents that the former 'latest shell succeeded' reconciliation was removed on purpose. So the fix cannot live at the terminal; it has to live at task acceptance.

next_step: Design a receipt-backed verification ledger keyed by (normalized target, normalized command) that `_handle_done` — or the path just before `task_failed` at askme.py:4309-4320 — may consult, using only `all_steps` receipts, never model assertions. Register it as a protocol change before any measured claim.

title: Guard asymmetry: a repeated harmless READ kills the attempt, a repeated WRITE only escalates thinking
detail: Second consecutive identical successful shell -> `_StepFlow.END_ATTEMPT` with `[stuck_loop] shell ...: same successful command repeated` (askme.py:3119-3130). Second consecutive identical successful read (same `_read_key`) -> END_ATTEMPT with `[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly` (askme.py:3170-3179). But a duplicate write/edit of the same target only sets `attempt.use_think = True` and returns NEXT_STEP (askme.py:3106-3112) — the attempt survives. So the cheapest, most harmless repetition (re-reading a file) is punished hardest, and the genuinely wasteful one (rewriting the same content) is not. This is exactly the shape of scheduled run 135's openrouter-smoke red: `test_create_and_read_file` -> status "exhausted" with `[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly`.

title: `dup_skip_count` is one counter shared across unrelated guards, so an earlier skip can make the FIRST duplicate shell/read fatal
detail: `dup_skip_count` is a single field on `TaskAttemptState` (askme.py:2592) incremented by the write/edit duplicate guard (3081), the shell duplicate guard (3119), the read duplicate guard (3170), the heuristic rewrite-loop guard (3299), and the lifecycle rewrite guard (3421). It is reset only in `_execute_step` (askme.py:4573, `attempt.dup_skip_count = 0  # reset on any non-skipped action`). Because the shell and read arms increment then immediately test `>= 2`, an attempt that already took one rewrite-loop skip enters the shell/read guard pre-armed: the very first duplicate shell or read then returns END_ATTEMPT with no corrective observation delivered to the model at all. Grep of tests/ found only `tests/test_agent_actions.py:1031 test_stuck_read_recorded_as_skipped` (asserting reasons == ['duplicate_read','stuck_read']) — the cross-guard priming case appears untested.

title: Suppressed steps enter the sliding window only — invisible to validation evidence, write visibility, and the final validator
detail: `StepRecorder.note(entry)` appends only to `state["last_steps"]` and its docstring says so explicitly: 'Model-visible corrective observation: enters the sliding window only, never the run-wide structured record or the JSONL log' (askme.py:2551-2554). `StepRecorder.record` is the one that also appends to `all_steps` (askme.py:2556-2563). `StepRecorder.skip` (2539-2549) only bumps `skipped_steps` and emits a JSONL skip event. Three consequences, all on the completion path: (1) `_has_new_validation_evidence` scans `all_steps` for an ok write/edit/shell after `validated_step_count`, so once validation has explicitly failed (`mark_failed`, askme.py:3708-3711) a run that only re-runs an already-successful check can NEVER meet the recheck precondition at askme.py:3746-3750 and is refused at 3824-3834; (2) `_write_visibility_flag` (askme.py:1730-1746) reports `{"no_write_executed": True}` for a task whose only actions were suppressed; (3) the validator's evidence lines are built from `completed_step_groups` (askme.py:2255-2266), which suppressed steps never enter.

next_step: If a receipt-backed verification ledger is built, source it from `all_steps` receipts only (never from `note` entries), and decide deliberately whether a suppressed-but-previously-successful command counts as 'new evidence' — the current answer is no, which is defensible but should be a stated decision, not an accident of which recorder method was called.

title: Duplicate detection is adjacency-only against `last_steps[-1]`, and `last_steps` carries across task boundaries
detail: `guard_duplicate` reads `last = controller.state["last_steps"][-1:]` and returns None immediately unless `last[0]["action"] == act` (askme.py:3017-3022). So the ban is not permanent: an already-succeeded command re-executes normally if ANY other action intervenes. Precise answer to 'can a task whose criterion is an already-succeeded command ever be satisfied without re-executing it?' — it can be satisfied by re-executing it (non-adjacently), or by the model emitting `done` after reading the corrective note 'Already ran successfully — use the earlier output. Take the next action, or emit done/fail.' (askme.py:3138-3141). What it cannot do is be satisfied from the record alone. Separately, `_execute_tasks` seeds each task with the previous task's final step (`prev_last = self.state["last_steps"][-1:]`, askme.py:4281, applied at 4343), so a new task's very FIRST action can be classified a duplicate of the previous task's last step when the args match exactly — the classic verify-only replan shape.

next_step: State the mechanism precisely in public: a 2-strike adjacency counter, not a permanent ban. Overclaiming 'the harness refuses to re-run successful commands' would be wrong.

title: Every listed coverage gap sits inside the completion / obligation / validation machinery
detail: Mapping the parent's uncovered ranges: askme.py 1483->1488 and 1494-1500 are `_extract_error_type`'s prefix parse and heuristic fallbacks — including line 1498 `return "stuck_loop", err`, the fallback classification of the very error string this whole failure mode produces (live errors already carry the `[stuck_loop]` prefix, so the fallback is effectively dead). 1551 is the `continue` when `_mutation_target_key` returns None inside `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` — the incomplete-write completion blocker. 1576-1583 is the non-dict/legacy branch and the `recovery_arg` fallbacks of the incomplete-write display helper; 1599 is `_next_pending_empty`'s 'all obligations allow append' fallback; 1674-1678 is `_pending_append_targets`' legacy `append_target` handling — all three feed the `[incomplete_write] ... completion refused` path at askme.py:4288-4296. 2172-2208 is `_should_validate`'s decision branches plus the head of `_deterministic_check` (pending_empty_writes, unresolved truncated writes, empty-file check). 2248-2272 is `_validate_completion`'s deterministic-False rejection and the evidence block it hands the validator. 3607-3632 is `WriteObligations`' truncated-write `pending_empty_writes` bookkeeping. So: yes, all of them — the aggregate 96.61% branch coverage conceals that the code deciding 'is this run complete' is the least-exercised region in the two runtime files.

Both correctly say these runs 'correctly end exhausted' per issue #68 and point at `AGENT_STEP_POLICY=lifecycle` as the untested lever. However docs/PERFORMANCE.md:576 says 'task 2 auto-done via duplicate guard' and the table at docs/PERFORMANCE.md:679-681 shows 'Write main.c loop (same content) | ... | 1 write → auto-done'. The current code does the opposite: askme.py:3115-3118 states 'Repetition is never completion evidence (issue #68): the duplicate is suppressed as a no-op once ... task acceptance still requires an explicit done.' Those are dated entries and legitimate history, but a blog post quoting that table would describe behavior the code no longer has.

title: The documented remedy (`AGENT_STEP_POLICY=lifecycle`) is stricter about `done`, not looser — it is not obviously the fix
detail: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:345 and docs/PERFORMANCE.md:179 both point at the lifecycle arm as 'the sanctioned lever to evaluate against this class'. But `LifecycleStepPolicy.guard_done` (askme.py:3387-3407) REFUSES `done` while `needs_verification` is set, emitting skip reason `lifecycle_unverified_done`; `needs_verification` is cleared only by a successful shell inside `note_result` (askme.py:3452-3454), which is called only from `_execute_step` (askme.py:4586) — never for a suppressed duplicate. It also refuses deterministic auto-completion (askme.py:3465-3468) and skips same-target rewrites (3409-3437, bumping the shared `dup_skip_count`). Direct adjacency deadlock is not trivially reachable (a write is always followed by an executable shell, since the guard only compares against the immediately previous step), but the arm strictly adds ways to refuse `done` on top of the guards that already cause exhaustion. Recommending it publicly as the remedy is not yet evidence-backed.

title: Issue #94 confirmed in code: no wire producer of incomplete_write exists after the tools-only migration
detail: Verified every link of #94's mechanism chain independently. (1) `_decode_tool_call_reply` (askme.py:1085-1125) is the sole executor-action decoder; on a payload cut at the token budget, `json.loads(raw_arguments)` raises and line 1117 raises `_tool_reply_error("tool call arguments are not valid JSON (truncated)")` — the entire envelope, content included, is discarded. (2) Its success path at line 1125 always constructs a DEFAULT `ActionTransport()`; there is no call site anywhere that builds `ActionTransport(content_truncated=True)` from a model reply. (3) `ctx.truncated_write = act == "write" and ctx.transport.content_truncated` (askme.py:3537) is therefore permanently False in a real run. (4) So `StepReceipt.executed(..., truncated_write=...)` never sets `_truncated_write` (actions.py:1058-1059) and `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` (askme.py:1539) never finds anything. NEW EVIDENCE #94 does not cite: `_RESERVED_ACTION_FIELDS = frozenset({"content_truncated", "finish_reason", "transport", "truncated_write"})` (actions.py:848-855) means a model that emitted `content_truncated` in its tool arguments is rejected by `parse_action_envelope`, closing the last theoretical wire path. The only surviving producer is askme.py:4498-4502, reachable only when the decoded action is a plain dict rather than a `DecodedAction` — i.e. an injected client.

title: CLAUDE.md's 'Truncation and observation integrity' invariant is the stale artifact, not ARCHITECTURE.md
detail: This is the key nuance a synthesis step must not get wrong. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is HONEST and current: its Interface revision 6 section (lines 186-206) states verbatim "The `content_truncated` intake, incomplete-write obligations, and chunked-append recovery remain for the structured run API and injected clients, but the wire decoder no longer produces partial content." It was updated in the removal commit itself (`git log -1 -- docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` -> 5e59dd6). By contrast CLAUDE.md:153-160 states "A partial/truncated mutation is `incomplete_write`, never a complete or merely unvalidated artifact. Preserve an actionable resume boundary and target" with no caveat, as an unconditional engineering invariant. A reader arriving from the talk reads CLAUDE.md/README first and will conclude the harness commits-and-resumes partial writes from live models. It does not. Likewise tests/workflows/PROTOCOL.md:74-82 describes the sentinel transport and resume-anchor recovery, but that text is explicitly scoped as 'revision-3 results' in a frozen protocol, so it is legitimately historical and should NOT be counted as stale.

title: The #41 C-header compile-repair heuristic is wired and ON BY DEFAULT — a confound in any public C-task claim
detail: `COMPILE_REPAIR_ENABLED = os.environ.get("AGENT_COMPILE_REPAIR", "1") == "1"` (askme.py:418) — default ON. It is fully wired end to end: `RunConfig.compile_repair` (askme.py:2820, read from env at 2851), resolved at 3988-3989, hash-logged into the run config payload at 4069, and dispatched at 4623-4624 via `_compile_repair_action(result.output, self.working_dir, action.get("arg", ""), enabled=self.compile_repair)`. The rule body is a hard-coded pattern table `_COMPILE_REPAIR_PATTERNS` (askme.py:2320-2341) that injects literal `#include <stdio.h>` and `#include <string.h>` on matching compile errors. The boundary conversion CLAUDE.md describes did land (it proposes a normal action through the executor), but the retain-vs-remove decision is still open per the roadmap. Practical consequence: every shipped run and every retained bench record ran with this heuristic ENABLED, so a public claim that a small local model 'fixed the C compile error' is partly a claim about a hardcoded lookup table.

title: #94's severity is profile-dependent: at the 8192-token default the discarded-write failure mode is far rarer
detail: Combining the two findings above: #94's dramatic live impact (a 3-call 256->512 escalation ladder producing nothing; T1b `exhausted` at 839 s with 6 of 7 executor steps failing `response_truncated`; T1a hitting the >1200 s wall clock) was measured on the 512-token legacy profile. On the default `generic-feature-scale-v1` profile with 8192 write tokens, a truncated write payload is much less likely, so the unreachable-recovery gap is mostly latent. This does NOT make #94 wrong — the code path is genuinely unreachable at any profile — but it means the public framing should be 'the recovery machinery has no live producer' (a correctness/honesty issue) rather than 'the harness is broken' (a reliability claim that the default config does not support).

The local primary is DENSE: docs/gemma4-setup.md:21 lists "Gemma 4 E4B QAT Q4_0 | models/gemma4-e4b-qat/gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf | 5.15 GB | Dense PLE, 4.5B effective / 8B incl. embeddings, iSWA | Full Metal | Primary (promoted 2026-08-03)", and docs/gemma4-setup.md:20 lists the legacy Q4_K_M at ~5.0 GB, also Dense PLE. What the owner most likely meant is one of two distinct things: (a) the SMALL DENSE local model (E4B QAT Q4_0) whose setup he wants reproduced on a runner, or (b) the MoE he already runs HOSTED — google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, which is the first berkeley-protocol cell in .github/workflows/llm.yml:33 and :154. A faithful "reproduce my local setup" lane must load (a): google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf / gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf, served by llama-server with the exact flags at docs/gemma4-setup.md:75-78 (-ngl 99 --ctx-size 16384 --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0 --swa-full --cache-reuse 256 --reasoning off) under capability profile legacy-e4b-m1-16k-v1 (docs/gemma4-setup.md:4, :90). It must NOT load 26B-A4B: at Q4 that is >=13.6 GB of weights before KV cache and does not fit any Apple Silicon runner GitHub offers. Publicly conflating the two would be the single most damaging error in the blog post, because the whole local-vs-hosted framing of the talk depends on the distinction.

title: No GitHub-hosted macOS runner can reproduce the M1 16 GB reference; the arithmetic rules out all three
detail: PR #96's macos.yml states the sizing directly in its header comment: "macos-26  M1, 3 vCPU, 7 GB — free/unlimited on public repos; macos-26-xlarge  M2 Pro, 5 vCPU, 14 GB — billed per-minute, always; macos-26-large  Intel, 12 vCPU, 30 GB — not Apple Silicon, no Metal". Memory need for the reference: 5.15 GB of weights resident under -ngl 99 (unified memory), plus a 16384-token q4_0 K+V cache with --swa-full (which deliberately disables the sliding-window KV savings), plus OS and Python. Verdict per runner: macos-26 (7 GB) NO — 5.15 GB of weights leaves under ~1.5 GB for KV, OS and the harness; it would swap or be OOM-killed, and PR #96 explicitly gates against this. macos-26-large (30 GB) NO for the purpose — it is Intel, so there is no Metal backend at all and -ngl 99 is meaningless; whatever it measured would be CPU inference, not the reference deployment. macos-26-xlarge (14 GB, M2 Pro) is the only candidate that holds the model, and it is still 2 GB below the 16 GB reference machine and a different chip generation. So the honest public statement is: the local M1 result is not reproducible on GitHub-hosted CI, and PR #96 says so in its own comment header ("No lane here produces performance evidence... timings from this workflow must never be written into docs/PERFORMANCE.md"). What PR #96's llama-reference lane provides instead is a FUNCTIONAL parity check on a runner label you supply: inputs are runner (default macos-26-xlarge), min_memory_gb (default "12"; set 16 to demand true parity), model_repo (default google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf), model_file (default gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf), model_revision (default main), and suite (easy/medium/hard). tests/ci_local_gate.py hardware runs the memory floor check BEFORE the 5.15 GB download so an undersized runner fails fast rather than looking like an agent-loop bug.

title: Even a successful reference run would not be binary-parity: it uses Homebrew llama.cpp, not the pinned local build b9618
detail: macos.yml's llama-reference lane installs the backend with `brew update --quiet && brew install llama.cpp` and only records `llama-server --version` afterwards. The documented local reference is a hand-built binary: docs/gemma4-setup.md:6 pins "Current local build: c34b92235 (build 9618, master as of 2026-06-13)" and warns "Do not replace stable b9618 without a side-by-side", gating a rebuild on upstream ggml-org/llama.cpp issue #26470 ("Metal Gemma-family decode regression, reported on M5/macOS 27 — M1 impact unknown"). Homebrew tracks upstream master and by 2026-08-30 is far ahead of b9618 (docs/gemma4-setup.md:7 already notes a fetched snapshot ee0445c99, 632 commits ahead of local). So a green reference lane proves "the local backend still works against current upstream llama.cpp" — which is exactly the drift signal the lane advertises — but it does NOT reproduce the local machine's inference stack, and any behavioral difference between it and the laptop is confounded by ~600+ upstream commits including a grammar/PEG overhaul and a suspected Metal Gemma decode regression. The server flags themselves DO match the doc exactly (macos.yml -ngl 99 --ctx-size 16384 --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0 --swa-full --cache-reuse 256 --reasoning off vs docs/gemma4-setup.md:75-78), and correctly omit --jinja because Gemma 4 has a dedicated llama.cpp parser.

title: What the two passing macOS runs on PR #96 actually established (and what they did not)
detail: Runs 33293229569 and 33293545613 (head 27dbfba) passed with three real jobs and one skip. Established, concretely: (1) ARM64 DETERMINISM — "Tests on Apple Silicon (Python 3.10)" and "(Python 3.14)" both green on macos-26, the deterministic suite running in ~41s and ~50s with no live-model opt-in, so conftest kept backend suites skipped. This proves the harness's platform-sensitive paths hold on macOS/arm64: /tmp and /var resolving through symlinks into /private, and a case-insensitive default filesystem — both of which bear directly on the workspace-path and target-identity normalization invariants in CLAUDE.md. It does NOT prove anything about model behavior, Metal performance, or the 16 GB reference. (2) LLAMA.CPP CONTRACT — "llama.cpp local-backend contract" green: brew install llama.cpp completed in ~64s, Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0 downloaded in ~154s with its x-repo-commit and sha256 recorded, llama-server became healthy in 5s under Metal, `ci_local_gate.py preflight` gated green, and the advisory `probe` step succeeded in 19s — i.e. a real tool call was decoded end-to-end through the actual LLMClient against a live Metal-backed llama-server. This proves the transport seam is intact on Apple Silicon and that the preflight closes conftest's silent-skip hole. It does NOT prove Gemma 4 works (different model, different parser path — Qwen needs --jinja, Gemma 4 does not), and the probe is explicitly advisory because a 0.6B model on 3 vCPU is not the reference deployment. (3) NOT established: the reference model never loaded (job skipped), so nothing about E4B QAT on CI, and nothing about performance — the workflow forbids its timings entering docs/PERFORMANCE.md.

title: OpenRouter wiring, precisely: one workflow, one environment, two jobs, four cells, two pinned dated snapshots, one identity gate
detail: Workflow: .github/workflows/llm.yml (name "LLM Tests"). Credential: environment secret OPENROUTER_API_KEY, scoped to the GitHub deployment environment named "Openrouter" (llm.yml:15-16, :69, :130); both jobs declare `environment: Openrouter`. Access guard (llm.yml:67 and :128, identical): the job runs only if the event is not a pull_request, OR the PR head repo equals the base repo AND the PR carries the 'llm-tests' label — so a fork PR is rejected before the credential is ever in scope, consistent with CLAUDE.md's credential rules. Jobs: openrouter-smoke (30 min, ubuntu-latest, runs TestOpenRouterEasy/Medium/Hard from tests/test_agent_integration.py, then asserts llm-logs/smoke.jsonl is non-empty so a silent skip cannot read as green) and berkeley-protocol (90 min, ubuntu-latest). Cells: 2 models x 2 tasks = 4. Models default (llm.yml:33, :154) to `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it=google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-20260403,qwen/qwen3.6-27b=qwen/qwen3.6-27b-20260422` — requested=expected-served syntax with an optional @low/@medium/@high effort suffix. Tasks: hard/test_replan_build_with_dependency and medium/test_fix_python_syntax_error, both under --reasoning-policy gated and --capability-profile generic-feature-scale-v1. Identity gate: --expected-served-model is passed to tests/bench_harness.py, which requires `metrics["served_models"] == [expected_served_model]` for a valid pass (tests/bench_harness.py:621) and refuses to run without it (bench_harness.py:501-503), so an OpenRouter route that quietly serves a different dated snapshot invalidates the cell rather than silently changing the result. Provider is 'auto' by default (llm.yml:37, :155) and the smoke job explicitly sets OPENROUTER_PROVIDER: "" with the comment "this checks the loop, not one provider's uptime".

title: The 'CI design defect, not code regression' claim is SUPPORTED by the config — with one correction: the reds are cell-correlated, not random
detail: Supported by the actual config. Trials: TRIALS defaults to "1" (llm.yml:41, :156) and is passed straight through as --trials to both bench_harness invocations (llm.yml:192, :199). Retries: grep for retry/continue-on-error/max-attempts in llm.yml returns ZERO matches — no step retries, no job retries, no re-roll. Pass rule: tests/ci_llm_gate.py:336, `passed = total > 0 and pytest_passed == total and agent_complete == total` — a cell is green only if EVERY trial is both a pytest pass and an agent completion, so at trials=1 a single non-claiming run reds the cell. Strictness asymmetry: --advisory-cell-failures is applied only when GITHUB_EVENT_NAME == "push" (llm.yml:212-214); scheduled runs, manual dispatches and PRs are STRICT. So the identical code that is advisory-green on a main push is hard-red on Monday's cron. That is exactly the shape of runs 132-135 (scheduled) vs run 130. Combined with issue #95's measured 11/20 (55%) claim-failure rate on work that was correct 20/20 and independently accepted, a 4-cell all-must-pass n=1 gate has a low ceiling on green even with zero regressions. CORRECTION to the claim: this is not "model variance." Run 135's two protocol failures were the SAME cell (medium/test_fix_python_syntax_error) on BOTH google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and qwen/qwen3.6-27b, while hard/test_replan_build_with_dependency passed on both — a correlated, task-specific failure, not a random draw. And the smoke failure was status "exhausted" with "[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly", which is the same mechanism family issue #95 documents ([stuck_loop] guard suppresses a redundant re-check, the task cannot be satisfied, the run exhausts despite finished work). So the accurate public sentence is: the gate design (n=1, no retries, all-cells-must-pass, strict on schedule) makes it maximally sensitive, and what it is sensitive TO is a real, reproducible completion-claiming defect (#95) rather than a change in askme.py or actions.py — git diff eee3fb7 fcd5bc0 leaves both runtime files byte-identical.

title: Provider routing is 'auto', so no two live runs are provider-matched — red-vs-green diffs are uninterpretable
detail: llm.yml:37 defaults provider to 'auto' and llm.yml:93-94 sets OPENROUTER_PROVIDER: "" for the smoke job with the comment "Automatic routing: this checks the loop, not one provider's uptime." That is a defensible choice for an uptime-insensitive smoke, but it means the serving provider behind google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it can differ between run 130 (green) and runs 132-135 (red) with no record-level control. CLAUDE.md requires "matched providers/configuration for causal comparisons." The gate does record served_providers (ci_llm_gate.py reads result["served_providers"] and renders a Provider column), so the artifacts from runs 130 and 135 can settle whether routing changed — but until someone reads those artifacts, "nothing changed in the code" is not the same as "nothing changed in the run." The served-MODEL identity gate (bench_harness.py:621) does close the snapshot-drift hole; it does not close the provider-drift hole.

title: incomplete_write / resume-anchor tests exercise a dead code path via the injection seam only — confirmed independently of issue #94
detail:
Issue #94's central claim is verified from the code here, not taken on trust. `ActionTransport(content_truncated=True)` is constructed at exactly one place in askme.py — line 4502, inside the explicitly-labelled legacy compatibility branch whose own comment says 'the real model decoder rejects the same key and returns DecodedAction instead' (askme.py:4494-4504). Every live decode call site passes a default transport: askme.py:1062 `_accept_or_raise(parsed, text)`, :1069 `_accept_or_raise(repaired, text)`, and the tools-transport path :1125 `_accept_or_raise(envelope, cleaned, ActionTransport())`. Since ACTION_TRANSPORT = 'tools' (askme.py:218) is the only transport post-#92 and the JSON-envelope sentinel prompt was removed (askme.py:587-588), `ctx.truncated_write = act == "write" and ctx.transport.content_truncated` (askme.py:3537) is always False in a real run, so `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` (askme.py:1539) never finds anything and `_completion_blocker` (askme.py:1645) never fires for truncation.

Every test that drives this machinery injects the state directly. `tests/test_agent_actions.py:1128 class TestTruncatedWriteContinuation` opens with `@patch("askme.ask_llm")` and a `side_effect` list whose second element is a raw dict: `{"action": "write", "arg": "impl.py", "content": "line1\nline2\nline3 par", "content_truncated": True}` (lines 1132-1141). That literal key is the injection seam — a model can never produce it. The same construction repeats at test_agent_actions.py lines 1175, 1214, 1250, 1277, 1301, 1332, 1764, 1948, 1980, 2012, 2053, 2059, 2115, 2122, 2165, 2209, 2219 and more (38 `content_truncated` occurrences in that one file). The seven tests in TestTruncatedWriteContinuation (test_partial_lines_written_then_append_completes, test_truncated_write_output_carries_resume_anchor, test_empty_truncated_write_not_told_to_append, test_empty_truncated_append_chunk_stays_append, test_line_boundary_truncation_drops_nothing, test_no_complete_line_skips_dispatch, test_reemitted_truncated_prefix_is_clean_restart) plus the symlink-alias obligation family (test_agent_actions.py:1937-2300) all depend on it. `tests/test_agent_step_policy.py`, `tests/test_agent_completion_gates.py`, and `tests/test_agent_run_state.py` reference `incomplete_write` a further 7 times, likewise from constructed state.

The damning part is that the suite ALSO pins the contradictory live behavior, in green, in a different file: `tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:253 test_exhausted_truncated_arguments_raise_response_truncated` feeds a genuinely cut tool-call payload (`'{"arg": "big.py", "content": "line one\\nline tw'`, finish_reason='length') and asserts `pytest.raises(json.JSONDecodeError, match="truncated")` with `response_truncated is True` — i.e. the whole write, content included, is discarded. So one suite certifies 'partial write is committed and resumed' and another certifies 'partial write is thrown away', and both pass.
evidence: askme.py:4494-4504 (only ActionTransport(content_truncated=True) construction; comment states the real decoder rejects the key) | askme.py:1062, 1069, 1125 (all live _accept_or_raise calls pass default/None transport) | askme.py:3537 ctx.truncated_write = act == "write" and ctx.transport.content_truncated | askme.py:218 ACTION_TRANSPORT = "tools"; askme.py:587-588 sentinel transport prompt removed | tests/test_agent_actions.py:1128-1360 class TestTruncatedWriteContinuation (7 tests, all via literal "content_truncated": True in mocked ask_llm dicts) | tests/test_agent_actions.py has 38 occurrences of content_truncated; test_agent_run_state.py 4, test_agent_step_policy.py 2, test_agent_completion_gates.py 1 | tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:238-259 (live path: truncated tool arguments -> JSONDecodeError, response_truncated=True, no write receipt) | github.com/den-run-ai/askme/issues/94
next_step: Before any public release, either land option 1 from #94 (salvage the valid prefix so a live truncated write actually produces _truncated_write) with a regression driven from a truncated tool-call reply rather than the injection seam, or land option 2 (delete the unreachable machinery, its ~50 injection-seam assertions, the CLAUDE.md invariant clause, and the docs/showcase-tasks.md claim). Do not ship a public repo where the largest single test class covers code no model can reach.

title: All 24 skips are live-backend tests, and the skip reason cannot distinguish 'not opted in' from 'backend down'
detail:
Full breakdown from `pytest tests/ -q -rs`. Group A — local llama-server on :8080, reason string 'live LLM tests not enabled or llama-server not running on :8080', 13 tests: tests/test_agent_integration.py lines 31, 40, 46, 62, 80, 100, 117, 134, 152, 366, 385, 411 and tests/test_agent_planning.py:424. Group B — OpenRouter, reason 'live LLM tests not enabled or OpenRouter API not available', 11 tests: tests/test_agent_integration.py lines 187, 195, 200, 214, 229, 246, 262, 278, 292, 318, 337. There is no third group; every skip is backend-gated, none are platform or dependency skips.

The gating logic (tests/conftest.py:71-82) is `pytest.mark.skipif(not live_llm_enabled or not _llm_available(), reason=...)`. Two separate conditions collapse into one reason string. Concretely: a contributor who sets ASKME_RUN_LIVE_LLM_TESTS=1 but has no llama-server running gets a skip line byte-identical to a contributor who never opted in. Nothing in the run output — not the reason, not a marker, not the count — distinguishes 'the backend was never asked' from 'the backend was asked and was unreachable'. For a project whose CLAUDE.md states 'A skipped integration suite is not evidence that a backend works', the harness cannot itself tell the two apart.

What IS defensible and worth saying: the short-circuit in `not live_llm_enabled or not _openrouter_available()` means Python never evaluates the probe when the env var is absent, so the default suite genuinely makes zero network calls and reads no credential — the network-free/credential-free claim in CLAUDE.md holds.
evidence: tests/conftest.py:71-82 (skip_no_llm, skip_no_openrouter skipif expressions and reason strings) | tests/conftest.py:36-45 _llm_available() probes http://localhost:8080/health | tests/conftest.py:48-68 _openrouter_available() reads repo-root .env then GETs openrouter.ai/api/v1/models | pytest tests/ -q -rs output: 1208 passed, 24 skipped, 13 llama-server + 11 OpenRouter
next_step: Split the two conditions into distinct reason strings ('ASKME_RUN_LIVE_LLM_TESTS not set' vs 'opted in but llama-server on :8080 unreachable'), and in any public README/blog copy state the pass count as '1208 deterministic, offline, mock-boundary tests; 24 live-backend tests skipped by default' rather than a bare '1208 passing'.

title: The repo's own documented commands fail on a stock machine: uv is pinned with == not >=
detail: pyproject.toml:22 sets `required-version = "==0.12.1"` under [tool.uv]. Every command block in CLAUDE.md and the README starts with `uv run --locked ...`. On this container (uv 0.8.17) the documented entry point fails immediately with: `error: Required uv version ==0.12.1 does not match the running version 0.8.17. Update uv by running uv self update 0.12.1`. This is not a stale-lock or a network issue — the exact-equality pin also rejects any uv NEWER than 0.12.1, so it will break again for every contributor on a current uv as soon as astral ships a release. A reader arriving from the recorded Berkeley talk and typing the first command in the README hits a hard error before anything runs. The workaround (invoke the venv interpreter directly) is undocumented.
evidence: pyproject.toml:20-22 [tool.uv] required-version = "==0.12.1" | observed: `uv run --locked --no-dev askme.py --help` -> error: Required uv version `==0.12.1` does not match the running version `0.8.17` | CLAUDE.md Commands section: every block begins with `uv run --locked` | .github/workflows/ci.yml:29,59 astral-sh/setup-uv pinned version: "0.12.1" (CI is consistent; only external contributors are affected)
next_step: Relax to `required-version = ">=0.12.1"` (CI already pins the exact version via setup-uv, so reproducibility is preserved), or add a documented plain-venv fallback path to the README quick start.

title: Issue #84's 30-second sleep is still there and is 82% of the deterministic suite's wall clock
detail:
Issue #84 scope item 1 asks to replace the real `sleep 60` with an injected subprocess.TimeoutExpired. It has not been done. `tests/test_agent_core.py:38-41` still reads: `def test_timeout(self, work_dir): result = execute({"action": "shell", "arg": "sleep 60"}, work_dir); assert result["ok"] is False; assert result["output"] == "TIMEOUT"`. It runs against the real production default `SHELL_TIMEOUT = 30` (actions.py:56). Measured in isolation: 30.15s. The whole suite is 36.67s, so this one case is ~82% of the runtime, and CI pays it five times (ubuntu-latest x Python 3.10-3.14, ci.yml:49). Issue #84's own estimate of '~6 seconds without the timeout' matches the residual almost exactly.

The broader consolidation in #84 has also not happened: collected cases are now 1232 (1208+24) versus the 1,132 baseline the issue records at b86e534, i.e. the suite grew by ~100 cases rather than consolidating. tests/test_agent_action_protocol.py + tests/test_agent_schemas.py still collect 269 cases together, and tests/_test_support.py exists but RunDependencies appears in only 3 test files (test_agent_run_api.py:6, test_agent_step_policy.py:2, test_agent_run_config.py:2).
evidence: tests/test_agent_core.py:38-41 (sleep 60) | actions.py:56 SHELL_TIMEOUT = 30  # default | measured: pytest tests/test_agent_core.py::TestExecuteShell::test_timeout -> 1 passed in 30.15s; full suite 36.67s | .github/workflows/ci.yml:49 matrix python-version 3.10-3.14, all ubuntu-latest | pytest --collect-only: 1232 cases vs issue #84's recorded 1,132 at b86e534 | github.com/den-run-ai/askme/issues/84
next_step: Land #84 scope item 1 alone as a small PR — inject subprocess.TimeoutExpired and separately assert the configured timeout value reaches subprocess.run. It cuts CI wall clock by ~150s across the matrix and is the single cheapest visible quality win before a public release.

title: The 90% coverage gate covers only askme.py and actions.py — the evidence-producing infrastructure is outside it
detail:
pyproject.toml [tool.coverage.run] sets `source = ["askme", "actions"]` with branch = true, and [tool.coverage.report] sets fail_under = 90. ci.yml:73-74 passes `--cov=askme --cov=actions` and runs coverage only on the Python 3.14 matrix leg (ci.yml:69, 81, 89). So the modules that produce the project's public evidence — tests/workflow_eval.py (the native semantic workflow evaluator), tests/bench_harness.py, tests/featurebench/askme_adapter.py, tests/featurebench/canary_audit.py, tests/ci_llm_gate.py — carry no coverage floor at all. They are type-checked (pyproject.toml [tool.ty.src] include lists all five) and they do have their own test files, but a regression in the evaluator or the canary audit cannot fail the coverage gate. For a project whose credibility rests on 'claims trace to frozen records', the record-producing code is the code least protected by the headline number.

The 96.61% figure is therefore accurate but narrower than a reader will assume: it describes the two runtime modules, not the harness as a whole.

title: Observation-integrity truncation coverage is real, reachable, and defensible to cite publicly
detail:
This is the counterweight to the incomplete_write finding and is worth stating in the blog post because it is the invariant most likely to be probed. Unlike the truncation-recovery family, the read/search/tree truncation tests call the production `execute(...)` against real files on disk and assert the user-visible contract. tests/test_agent_actions.py carries explicit `truncation_reasons` assertions for every documented cap: 'matches' (:272), 'snippets' (:291), 'files' (:300), 'chars' (:308, :438), 'unreadable' (:348), 'entries' (:407), 'depth' (:428), 'walk_errors' (:463) — and, critically, negative cases asserting `truncation_reasons == []` when no cap was hit (:285, :317, :415), which is what makes the positive assertions meaningful.

Continuation resume-reconstruction is likewise covered against reconstructed artifacts, not internal flags: test_window_header_and_continuation (:69), test_continuation_navigation_covers_whole_file (:80), test_last_window_has_no_continuation (:88), test_offset_past_eof (:95), test_long_single_line_reconstructs_exactly (:124), test_wide_multiline_pages_reconstruct_to_eof (:134), test_nondefault_limit_is_preserved_through_reconstruction (:144), test_stale_hash_rejects_continuation (:165), test_cursor_requires_valid_continuation_limit (:182). These match the CLAUDE.md invariant clause by clause ('long lines, wide multi-line windows, repeated continuation to EOF').

title: No assertion-free or trivially-passing tests found — the one AST candidate is a false positive
detail:
An AST scan of every `test_*` function in tests/test_*.py for functions containing zero ast.Assert nodes returned 44 hits. 43 of them are `pytest.raises`/`pytest.warns` with-block tests, which is the correct idiom (e.g. tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:202-227, tests/test_agent_run_config.py:70-169). The single remaining candidate, tests/test_agent_integration.py:292 test_replan_multi_step_recovery, has no inline assert and no with-block — but it ends in `assert_file(tmp_path / "config.json", "SUCCESS")`, a module helper that does assert. So it can fail. There is no `assert True`, no bare `pass` test, and no xfail in the suite; xfail_strict = true and filterwarnings = ["error"] are set in pyproject.toml, so a warning is a failure and an unexpectedly-passing xfail would be an error. On the specific charge 'assertions that cannot fail', the repo is clean and this can be said publicly.

One residual caveat: tests/test_agent_actions.py contains 13 inline `pytest.skip("file/directory symlinks are unavailable")` guards (lines 61, 345, 1891, 1973, 2005, 2045, 2103, 2157, 2192, 2268, 2315, 2362, 2417). CI is ubuntu-only (ci.yml:18, 44), so they never trip there, but a contributor on a symlink-restricted Windows checkout silently loses the entire symlink-alias identity-normalization family with no signal beyond a higher skip count.

title: CLAUDE.md invariants without test coverage are narrow — the notable gap is the recovery half of the incomplete_write rule
detail: Walking the 'Engineering invariants' block against the suite: (a) Truncation and observation integrity — the observation half (bounded read/search/tree must not look complete) is covered and reachable; the mutation half ('A partial/truncated mutation is incomplete_write... Preserve an actionable resume boundary and target') is covered only through the injection seam and is unreachable in production, per the release-blocker finding above. (b) Continuations must resume at the first unread content, reconstructed without gaps or duplication — covered and reachable (test_agent_actions.py:80-182). (c) 'An explicit validator rejection cannot be erased by a later unavailable or malformed validator response. Require new successful mutation or shell evidence before a recheck' — covered: tests/test_agent_recovery.py:1477 test_validate_unavailable_is_complete_unverified, :1527 test_validate_recheck_capped_after_recovery, :1559 test_validate_recheck_requires_new_evidence. (d) 'Do not add workspace mutations, including deterministic recovery, that bypass the action/recording boundary' (#41) — covered: tests/test_agent_recovery.py:969 test_proposed_action_is_executor_valid_and_repairs_the_file, tests/test_agent_completion_gates.py:39 test_repair_auto_completion_cannot_bypass_an_open_obligation. (e) 'Never leak held-out evaluator evidence into prompts' — held-out handling appears only in tests/test_workflow_eval.py and tests/workflow_eval.py; I did not verify whether a test asserts that held-out evidence never reaches the agent's recovery context, and that module is outside the coverage gate. So the one invariant with a demonstrated coverage-vs-reachability gap is the incomplete_write recovery half; (e) is the one I could not confirm either way.

title: conftest silently sources a repo-root .env into os.environ when live tests are opted in
detail: tests/conftest.py:52-58: `_openrouter_available()` reads `<repo root>/.env` line by line and calls `os.environ.setdefault(k, v)` for every KEY=VALUE line before checking OPENROUTER_API_KEY. This only executes when ASKME_RUN_LIVE_LLM_TESTS=1 (short-circuit at conftest.py:78), so the default suite is unaffected and the network-free claim holds. But it means the opt-in path injects arbitrary key/value pairs from an untracked dotfile into the process environment of the whole test session, not just the OpenRouter credential, and it does so as a side effect of a function named `_openrouter_available`. For a public repo where readers will copy the live-test invocation, that is worth either narrowing to OPENROUTER_API_KEY or documenting.
evidence: tests/conftest.py:48-68 _openrouter_available() reads .env and os.environ.setdefault for every line | tests/conftest.py:71-82 short-circuit means the .env read never happens without the opt-in
next_step: Narrow the .env parse to the single OPENROUTER_API_KEY key, or move it to an explicitly named helper so the side effect is visible at the call site.
